assessment.nobel_worthiness: The first direct images of black-hole shadows (M87*, later Sgr A*) turn an object I have worked on theoretically into something nature lets us look at. It tests strong-field gravity at the horizon scale, with an elegant combination of very-long-baseline interferometry, calibration and imaging. The clarity and public meaning are exceptional, and this is a discovery rather than a model.
assessment.attribution: Falcke supplied the shadow-imaging concept and scientific case, Doeleman led the technical and collaborative realisation of the global mm-VLBI array, and Zensus built the European and institutional base. This is a plausible triple, but the work is the product of a large collaboration and a fair prize configuration is the hardest part.
assessment.maturity: The M87* result (2019) has been followed by polarization results and the independent Sgr A* image, with consistent ring size and consistent interpretation. Recognition is timely, although the GR tests remain coarse at present.
uncertainties: Large-collaboration credit and the roles of other leaders (not on this list) are hard to adjudicate; I rely on recalled history, not verified documents.
Precision of gravity tests from the shadow size is still modest, and some astrophysical modelling (accretion flow) is degenerate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental discovery of the scalar boson completed the Standard Model and is one of the great clues-from-nature results. The 2013 prize recognised the theory; the experimental confirmation by two independent detectors is a distinct and landmark achievement, and the Higgs couplings are now a central measurement programme.
assessment.attribution: Only three of the four credited names can be chosen. Jenni (ATLAS founding figure) and Virdee (CMS leading figure) represent the two experiments' conception and construction, and Gianotti led ATLAS at the time of the 2012 announcement. Della Negra is an equally defensible alternative on the CMS side, and the Nobel statutes make a collaboration-based award awkward.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature: more than a decade of confirmation, the mass and spin-parity are established, and several couplings are measured. Timing is, if anything, overdue.
uncertainties: Collaboration size makes choosing three people contentious; the committee has historically been reluctant to credit experiments' leaders.
Whether the Higgs discovery can be recognised again so soon after the 2013 theory prize is a procedural question I cannot resolve from the longlist.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: IceCube detected a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos at TeV-PeV energies, and then pointed to sources (the TXS 0506+056 blazar flare, the Seyfert galaxy NGC 1068, and the Galactic plane). This opens neutrino astronomy with a cubic-kilometre detector built in Antarctic ice, a real instrumental and scientific achievement and an existential extension of our view of the universe.
assessment.attribution: Halzen is the intellectual driver and principal investigator of the project and Karle is a central figure in the detector and construction. Both are credited, which gives a clean two-person configuration. Other major figures of the collaboration, including project leadership across institutions, are not on the list, so I cannot judge their relative claim from the supplied text.
assessment.maturity: The discovery signal (2013) is by now supported by multiple analyses and by source-association evidence. Source identification is still at a modest significance level for individual objects, so this is a strong but not fully complete picture.
uncertainties: Point-source evidence is at the few-sigma level and the origin of the diffuse flux is not fully resolved.
Only two credited names; recognition of other founders is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Katori's magic-wavelength insight made optical lattice clocks possible, and Ye's work took them to the 10^-18 level of precision. These clocks test fundamental constants and relativity (gravitational redshift at millimetre scales), will drive a redefinition of the second, and are a nature-facing instrument. The Hall and Hansch frequency-comb prize (2005) and Wineland's ion-clock work (2012) form natural predecessors.
assessment.attribution: The two credited names are the clear decisive contributors: Katori for the concept and first demonstration, and Ye for the demonstration of record accuracy and the strontium clock programme. This is a clean two-person prize.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with independent confirmation in many laboratories, and a redefinition of the SI second under discussion. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Competition from trapped-ion optical clock work, which has already been recognised in part, may split the field's credit.
Whether the committee regards metrology as a leading frontier in physics.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The acoustic peaks in the CMB anisotropy and their precision mapping (WMAP, then Planck) fixed the parameters of the standard cosmological model and gave clear observational evidence for dark matter and dark energy, which is the topic that I find most interesting from my own theoretical work. The COBE prize (2006) and Peebles (2019) cover earlier steps; the precision era is not yet recognised.
assessment.attribution: Bennett (WMAP principal investigator), Spergel (WMAP theory and parameter inference) and Puget (Planck HFI lead) give two independent satellite programmes and the interpretation. Page and Sunyaev are strong alternatives, so the credit allocation is genuinely unresolved.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature, with independent confirmation by WMAP, Planck and ground-based experiments. The persistent Hubble-tension is a puzzle but does not undermine the discovery.
uncertainties: Five credited names for a three-person limit; the decisive contributors among them are debatable.
Partial overlap with the previous cosmology prizes could make the committee see this as already honoured.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Bistritzer-MacDonald flat-band prediction and the Jarillo-Herrero group's discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened a whole field (moire materials) in which theory predicted a clue that nature then confirmed. The theory-experiment pairing is what I appreciate.
assessment.attribution: The pairing of prediction (Bistritzer, MacDonald) and experimental discovery (Jarillo-Herrero) is clear, so all three credited names make a coherent prize. Cao and others in the experimental group are not on the list, which leaves some attribution uncertainty.
assessment.maturity: Many groups have reproduced the correlated phases, but the interpretation of the superconductivity mechanism and the role of other phases remains debated. The field is fast moving, so the recognition may be slightly early.
uncertainties: The superconducting mechanism is not settled.
Sample dependence and reproducibility in the early years; the credit of early student and postdoctoral contributors is not in the supplied text.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The detection of the first transiting exoplanet, HD 209458b, and then of sodium in its atmosphere, moved exoplanet science from detection of existence to physical characterisation. It follows the 2019 prize for the discovery of exoplanets, and the atmospheric step has the existential dimension I mentioned in public: we can now study the chemistry of other worlds.
assessment.attribution: Henry's group independently detected the transit, Charbonneau and Brown led the HST characterisation and the atmospheric sodium detection. The three-person split seems fair, but the credit is entangled with the Mayor-Queloz-honoured radial velocity discovery and with the broader transit-photometry community.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many subsequent transit surveys and by JWST-era spectroscopy. Mature, though the compound nature (transit discovery plus atmosphere) means the two parts have different significance.
uncertainties: Possible overlap with the 2019 prize and uncertainty over whether the transit part or the atmospheric part is the core of the discovery.
Other exoplanet-atmosphere pioneers appear in other candidates (the separate exoplanet-atmosphere entry) and the credit may be better placed there.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Pulsar-timing evidence for a nanohertz gravitational-wave background, probably from supermassive black-hole binaries, opens a new gravitational-wave band and links back to the black holes and cosmology that I care about. It is a result that comes from nature and not from taste.
assessment.attribution: The credit is spread across several PTA collaborations (EPTA, NANOGrav, PPTA, and others). Manchester (PPTA, pulsar timing), Kramer (EPTA, pulsar physics) and McLaughlin (NANOGrav) represent three of the main groups, but Siemens, who led the NANOGrav analysis, is an equally plausible choice, so the attribution is genuinely open.
assessment.maturity: The 2023 evidence is at roughly 3-4 sigma for the Hellings-Downs correlation and the source interpretation (supermassive binaries versus new physics) is not settled. Recognition is likely premature, which is why it is placed at the bottom of my eight.
uncertainties: Significance of the signal and its astrophysical origin are not yet established.
The multi-collaboration structure makes a three-person award difficult.
